analysis.one_liner: Modernizes voter registration with automatic and same-day registration, expands early and mail voting, and protects ballot access.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee hearing or floor vote; it died at the end of the 118th Congress with 14 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would overhaul how Americans register and vote in federal elections: automatic registration through motor vehicle, Medicaid, and other government agencies unless a person declines; online registration and updates in every state; same-day registration; minimum periods of early voting; voting by mail on request; paper ballots with a hand-marked or verified option; limits on purging voters based on multi-state record matches; and new protections for voters with disabilities, voters on tribal lands, overseas and military voters, and people who have finished felony sentences. It also funds states and local election offices to implement these changes. It was introduced in September 2024, sent to six House committees, and received no hearing or vote before the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters who find registration burdensome: young people, frequent movers, low-income households interacting with Medicaid or benefits agencies, voters with disabilities, voters on tribal lands, military and overseas voters, and citizens returning from incarceration. Election offices also gain funding and clearer federal standards.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters, especially young, low-income, disabled, and mobile ones

how_it_helps.text: Every state must register eligible citizens automatically through agencies like motor vehicle authorities, Medicaid, and Social Security unless the individual declines, and must let 16- and 17-year-olds be pre-registered [S2].
Every state must offer online registration, online updates to registration information, same-day registration at the polls, early voting, and voting by mail in federal elections [S2].

States may not remove a voter from the rolls based on an interstate cross-check unless they have full name, date of birth, and the last four digits of the Social Security number confirming the match, or ERIC documentation that the voter has moved [S2].

The bill requires accessible election websites, protects in-person voting for people with disabilities and older voters, expands grants for disability voting access, and permits private independent registration for disabled voters at home [S2].

It requires polling place accessibility, secured ballot drop boxes, curbside voting, accommodations for voters on Indian lands, and a sworn written statement as an alternative to photo identification [S2].
It restores federal voting rights to citizens after they complete a criminal sentence and notifies them of that restoration [S2].
It authorizes $500 million in grants to states for implementing automatic registration, plus grants for poll worker recruitment and for involving young people in elections [S2].

analysis.who_pays: State election administrators bear the cost of new registration systems, early voting periods, mail voting, and paper ballot requirements, offset partly by federal grants; taxpayers fund roughly $500 million or more in implementation grants; states that require photo ID lose the ability to insist on it; and parties and campaigns that rely on restrictive registration and voting rules lose those levers.
analysis.who_pays_short: State election offices and federal taxpayers

drawbacks.text: Automatic registration through agency records raises data-quality concerns: if an agency record is wrong or out of date, a voter can be registered at an incorrect address, and the bill specifically shields individuals from prosecution for being automatically registered at the wrong address, which critics say weakens list accuracy incentives [S2].

The bill sets a floor of federal election rules on states, overriding state-specific choices on registration deadlines, voter ID, early voting periods, and purging practices; states' rights advocates object to this federal preemption [S2].
Implementation costs for states are substantial, and while the bill authorizes grants, it does not guarantee appropriations to cover the full cost of new systems and expanded voting periods [S2].

Restoring voting rights immediately after sentence completion, rather than after victims' restitution or parole compliance in some states, is opposed by those who believe disenfranchisement should last longer [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For eligible citizens, the benefit is large: registration becomes automatic or same-day, and barriers like ID rules, limited early voting, and aggressive purges shrink. The costs are real but bounded: implementation spending and a loss of state discretion over election rules. The design includes fraud safeguards (prosecution remains available for knowing false registration or voting) and data-security standards, though automatic registration data quality is a genuine weak point. On balance the costs are administrative and the gains broad.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in the House in September 2024 and referred to six committees; the House never took it up before the Congress ended in January 2025 [S4].

narrative.text: Rep. James Clyburn introduced the bill on September 20, 2024, near the end of the 118th Congress [S1].
It was referred to six committees, with House Administration the lead, a structure that usually signals no committee intends to act quickly [S4].
The bill had 14 cosponsors, all Democrats [S3].
No hearing, markup, or floor vote is recorded in the action history, and the bill expired when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State officials and groups who prefer decentralized election rules are better off, since no federal registration or voting-access mandate took effect; voters who would have benefited from automatic and same-day registration gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. James Clyburn
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and organized 14 Democratic cosponsors [S1][S3].

against.name: House leadership and committee chairs (Republican majority)
against.role: Controlled the House schedule and committees in the 118th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or vote; the bill sat in six committees until the Congress ended [S4].

sides.party_line_note: All 15 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the Republican House majority took no action [S3][S4].

industries.note: The bill would create demand for online registration systems, electronic signature transfer, ballot tracking, and paper ballot printing equipment, paid for partly by federal grants; but it also imposes federal standards that could complicate vendor contracts with states [S2].
They would receive funding and clearer national standards but also new unfunded mandates and loss of discretion over registration, ID, and purging rules [S2].
